problems.description: Module-level shared connection with check_same_thread=False: under Flask's default threaded dev server all requests share one sqlite connection, which can interleave transactions; per-request connections or a connection-per-thread is the more idiomatic Flask+SQLite pattern.

DATABASE default changed to ':memory:' — a shared in-memory DB loses all data on restart and is wiped between connections; acceptable for tests but a questionable production default since the DB is now created at import time with no reconnect logic.

Convention score 0.71 mostly reflects violations in untouched files (celery_config.py, notifications.py, repositories.py, and PascalCase/case flags in the pre-existing codebase). The commit's own delta (app.py edits + new test_app.py) is largely clean; the measurement penalizes pre-existing state, not this commit.

strengths: Solid test suite covering CRUD, ordering (newest-first), 400 on blank/missing title, and JSON 404 for missing task
Title input hardening (isinstance check before .strip()) prevents AttributeError on non-string JSON payloads
Module-level init_db() ensures schema exists before serving, and the added conn.commit() makes schema creation explicit
Pattern change (connection + row_factory) is consistent and preserves the env-var override for DATABASE
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, well-tested greenfield session whose main risk is the shared module-level in-memory connection under a threaded server, and whose 0.71 convention score is inflated by pre-existing violations in files this commit never touched.

problems.description: Default DB is ':memory:' with a single shared connection; under a multi-process/worker deployment each process gets a fresh empty DB, so registered users and their tasks silently vanish and auth breaks entirely at runtime.

Auth feature added with no tests (+1 file only, test_app.py untouched), despite test_app.py existing; owner-scoping and token verification are exactly the kind of logic that needs regression coverage.
JWT_SECRET falls back to a hardcoded 'development-secret-change-me'; if deployed without the env var, all tokens are forgeable with a well-known secret.
No rate limiting or lockout on /auth/login; password brute-force is unbounded.

strengths: Owner-scoped queries (WHERE owner_id = ?) on every task endpoint correctly prevent cross-user data access and account for tenant isolation.
All SQL is parameterized; no injection surface added.
Idiomatic auth: werkzeug for password hashing, @require_auth decorator with @wraps preserving function metadata, JWT payload validated with algorithms pinned.
Migration handled via PRAGMA table_info check with ALTER TABLE for pre-existing DBs rather than forcing a drop.
SonarQube delta confirms quality improved: smells -4, cognitive complexity -8, no new bugs or duplications.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, pattern-respecting JWT auth + per-user task scoping feature that improves code quality (smells -4, complexity -8) and adds real tenant isolation, but ships without tests and leans on an in-memory default DB and a hardcoded dev secret that undermine the feature's correctness in production.

problems.description: send_notification_email.delay() is called unguarded in the edit_task route; if the Redis broker is unreachable, completing a task raises and returns a 500 even though the update itself succeeded.

Notification trigger logic is embedded in the route handler rather than a small transition helper, and the task-not-found check is now duplicated (explicit pre-check plus the existing post-update check).
email = email or username silently conflates email and username; a missing email surfaces as a notification addressed to the username.

strengths: Async notification is cleanly separated into notifications.py with an explicit Celery route to a dedicated queue
Migration-safe schema change via PRAGMA table_info + ALTER TABLE preserves existing databases
Tests cover the enqueue behavior including the no-duplicate-email-on-second-update edge case
commit_reviews.summary: A well-integrated session that adds async email notifications and fixes the edit_task 404 gap, with the main caveats being an unguarded Celery call and a convention score (0.71) inflated by lint flags largely not introduced by this diff (repositories.py is untouched, no new classes added).

problems.description: Inconsistent migration: register/add_task routes call user_repository()/task_repository() directly while create_user/find_user/create_task helpers remain in app.py, creating two parallel code paths for the same operations
Cognitive complexity increased by +27 (per SonarQube), concentrated in the new generic BaseRepository.create(**fields) dynamic-SQL builder and repository layer
Refactor added a 155-line repository layer with no new tests; behavior relies entirely on existing test_app.py coverage
Password hashing stays in the app layer (create_user passes generate_password_hash result into the repository) rather than being encapsulated with user persistence

repositories.py flagged for module-level constants not UPPER_CASE (per convention score 0.71); remaining violations are pre-existing in celery_config.py/notifications.py/test_app.py, not introduced here
Repository factory functions (user_repository/task_repository) fetch a fresh get_db() connection per call; acceptable for SQLite per-request use but redundant when a route touches a repository twice

strengths: Extracts ~85 lines of inline SQL out of app.py into a dedicated repositories.py module, cleanly separating data access from route logic
Idiomatic Repository pattern: BaseRepository ABC with abstract table_name property, generic create() helper, and typed TaskRepository/UserRepository subclasses
Behavior-preserving refactor per measurements: bugs +0, duplications +0.0%, function signatures and route behavior intact
Follows project conventions: PascalCase classes, snake_case methods, type hints on public signatures, docstrings on public API
commit_reviews.summary: A solid, behavior-preserving Repository-pattern refactor that slims app.py and improves separation of concerns, slightly marred by an incomplete migration that leaves dual code paths and a +27 cognitive complexity bump.

problems.description: list_for_owner ordering silently changed from created_at DESC to id DESC, altering a shared repository method's semantics to serve the new cursor pagination; couples endpoint ordering to row id rather than the documented creation timestamp.
Rate limiter pulls in a Redis default (REDIS_URL) for a baseline SQLite/in-memory app; the in-memory fallback mitigates it, but it changes the deployment surface for a simple baseline service.
list_page_for_owner issues a full COUNT(*) on every page request — fine for the baseline dataset but O(n) per request as rows grow.

test_rate_limit_returns_retry_after_header fires 101 sequential requests and is hard-coupled to the 100/min default limit and module-level limiter state, making it slow and brittle to config changes or test ordering.
list_tasks handler grew validation and pagination branches inline (consistent with measured cognitive complexity +19); the cursor/limit parsing could be a small helper to keep the route thin.

strengths: Keyset/cursor pagination (id < cursor) instead of OFFSET — scales correctly and avoids page-drift.
Rate limiting keyed on the authenticated user with IP fallback, returning proper 429 with Retry-After header.
Input validation for cursor/limit returns clean 400s before touching the DB.
Solid test coverage: pagination page boundaries, invalid parameters, Retry-After header, and updated response-shape assertions.
Follows existing conventions: new wrapper functions mirror get_task/get_tasks, reuses BaseRepository.find_all, and reuses the authenticated_client/auth_header test fixtures.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, well-tested commit that adds correct keyset pagination and user-aware rate limiting while following repository/test patterns, though the 0.71 measured convention score is dragged down mostly by pre-existing violations in untouched files (celery_config.py, notifications.py) rather than this commit's own code.

compounding_issues: Session 3 added Celery email notification via `.delay()`, but no Celery worker is ever started and the task is a mock print — the feature is inert without an external Redis broker+worker, an infra dependency later sessions never resolved.

Session 2 changed the DATABASE default from `todos.db` to `:memory:`, so the ALTER TABLE migration scaffolding added in sessions 2/3 (for preserving existing data) is dead code against an in-memory store; data persistence was silently dropped and never revisited.

Session 4's repository refactor was left half-done: app.py still carries dead helper functions (`create_user`, `create_task`, `get_tasks`) alongside direct repository calls in routes, plus a duplicate notification-email default fallback that relies on email being seeded to username.
Hardcoded `JWT_SECRET` fallback (`development-secret-change-me`) and `app.run(debug=True)` carried from session 2 into the final commit as unresolved security debt.

Session 5 switched list ordering from `created_at DESC` to `id DESC` and bolted on a Redis-backed rate limiter, accumulating another external dependency on the same broker used by Celery, increasing operational fragility.
key_decisions: Session 2: introduce JWT auth (register/login/`require_auth`) with per-user `owner_id` scoping on all task queries — the single most consequential decision, making multi-tenancy the core domain invariant every later session builds on.
Session 2: switch from per-call SQLite connections to one global `:memory:` connection, sacrificing persistence for test determinism.
Session 3: add Celery + Redis for async completion emails, extending the schema with `email` via idempotent ALTER TABLE migrations.
Session 4: extract a generic `BaseRepository`/`TaskRepository`/`UserRepository` data-access layer, moving SQL out of app.py into `repositories.py`.
Session 5: replace full-list returns with keyset cursor pagination (id-based, `next_cursor`/`total`) and add per-user rate limiting keyed off the JWT `sub` claim.
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved across the five sessions, rising from a minimal single-file CRUD seed through well-tested multi-tenancy (session 2) to a structured repository-backed service with pagination and rate limiting (sessions 4-5), with tests consistently expanded and kept green at each step. The arc is coherent — auth in session 2 enabled per-user scoping in 4 and per-user pagination/limits in 5 — and session 5 builds naturally on the session 4 repository seam rather than re-plumbing it. The arc is not monotonic: session 3's Celery notification adds infrastructure weight disproportionate to a mock email, and session 4's refactor leaves dead helpers behind, so the gains are real but accompanied by accumulating external dependencies and unfinished cleanup that later sessions never paid down.
story_review.summary: A coherent greenfield-to-polish progression where early auth and per-user scoping decisions compound well into later pagination and rate-limiting work, though the arc accretes unresolvable Redis/Celery dependencies, a dead in-memory migration path, and partially-completed refactor debt.
